items.title: Suspended means taken away for now
items.simple: The court or DMV can suspend your license if you break certain laws or break laws repeatedly. Suspended means you lose the right to drive for a while. You pay fees to get your license back when the suspension ends.
items.official: If you break certain laws or repeatedly violate the laws of Virginia, your driving privilege may be suspended or revoked by the court and/or DMV. If your license is suspended, your privilege to drive has been withdrawn temporarily. You may pay the required fees and reinstate your license at the end of the suspension period.
items.mnemonic: Suspended = paused. Revoked = ended.

items.title: Reinstating after a suspension
items.simple: To get your license back, you must show proof of legal presence. If your license was expired for one year or more during the suspension, you must also pass the knowledge, road skills and vision exams.
items.official: You will be required to show proof of legal presence, which means you are either a U.S. citizen or legally authorized by the federal government to be in the U.S. During the suspension period, if your license has been expired for one year or more, you must show proof of legal presence and pass the two-part knowledge, road skills and vision exams to have your driving privilege reinstated.
items.mnemonic: Expired a year or more? Test again.

items.title: Revoked means ended; re-apply
items.simple: Revoked means your right to drive has ended. When the revocation period is over, you must apply again. You must show legal presence, pass the vision, knowledge and road skills tests, and pay fees.
items.official: Revocation means that your privilege to drive has been terminated. Your driving privilege may be restored if you re-apply for a driver's license and show proof of legal presence after the revocation period has passed. You must successfully complete the vision screening, two-part knowledge exam and road skills tests and pay the required fees when you re-apply.
items.mnemonic: Revoked = start over from the beginning.

items.title: DUI always costs your license
items.simple: If you are convicted of DUI, your license will be suspended or revoked. That is also true for hurting someone while driving under the influence, for driving while suspended for DUI, and for driving without a required ignition interlock.
items.official: The court or DMV will suspend or revoke your privilege to drive if you are convicted of: operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs (DUI); injuring another person as a result of operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs; operating a motor vehicle while suspended or revoked for a DUI; operating a motor vehicle that is not equipped with the ignition interlock device when it is required by the court or DMV.
items.mnemonic: DUI means you WILL lose your license.

items.title: Lying to DMV costs your license
items.simple: Never lie to DMV. A false statement means your license will be suspended or revoked. Do not take a license exam for someone else. Do not appear for someone else to renew their license.
items.official: The court or DMV will suspend or revoke your privilege to drive if you are convicted of: making a false statement to DMV; taking a driver's license exam for another person, or appearing for another person to renew a license.
items.mnemonic: At DMV, tell the truth and be only you.

items.title: Injury crash: stop and identify
items.simple: If someone is hurt or killed in your crash, you must stop and tell who you are. If you leave, your license will be suspended or revoked.
items.official: The court or DMV will suspend or revoke your privilege to drive if you are convicted of failing to stop and identify yourself at the scene of a crash if someone has been injured or killed.
items.mnemonic: Someone hurt? Stop and say who you are.

items.title: Manslaughter, drugs, felonies
items.simple: Some crimes always cost you your license. One is manslaughter caused by driving a vehicle. Others are a drug crime involving a vehicle and any felony in which you used a vehicle.
items.official: The court or DMV will suspend or revoke your privilege to drive if you are convicted of: voluntary or involuntary manslaughter resulting from driving a motor vehicle; involuntary manslaughter resulting from operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol; committing a motor vehicle-related drug offense; committing a felony involving the use of a motor vehicle.

items.title: Eluding police costs your license
items.simple: When police stop you, pull to the side of the road in a safe place and park. Running from police is called eluding. If you are convicted of eluding, your license will be suspended or revoked.
items.official: The court or DMV will suspend or revoke your privilege to drive if you are convicted of eluding police.
items.mnemonic: Elude police, lose your license.

items.title: Reckless or aggressive: court may act
items.simple: If you are convicted of reckless or aggressive driving, the court may suspend or revoke your license. The court gets to choose.
items.official: The court may suspend or revoke your driving privilege if you are convicted of the following offenses: reckless or aggressive driving.
items.mnemonic: DUI list = WILL lose it. Reckless list = MAY lose it.

items.title: No license or suspended: court may
items.simple: Do not drive without a valid license. Do not drive while your license is suspended or revoked for a reason other than DUI. If you are convicted, the court may suspend or revoke your license.
items.official: The court may suspend or revoke your driving privilege if you are convicted of: operating a motor vehicle without a valid driver's license; driving while your license is revoked or suspended for a non-DUI related conviction.

items.title: Refusing a blood or breath test
items.simple: If you are charged with DUI and you refuse a blood or breath test, the court may suspend or revoke your license. If you refuse a breath test, your license is also suspended automatically.
items.official: The court may suspend or revoke your driving privilege if you are convicted of refusing to take a blood/breath test when charged with driving while under the influence of alcohol/drugs. If you refuse a breath test and law enforcement charges you with driving while under the influence of alcohol/drugs, your driving privilege will be automatically suspended.

items.title: Demerit points: 3, 4 or 6
items.simple: Each traffic conviction adds 3, 4 or 6 demerit points to your DMV record. DMV counts how many points you get in 12 months and in 24 months.
items.official: When convictions are added to your record, DMV assigns demerit points to traffic offenses and moving violations. DMV also monitors your driving record to see how many demerit points you receive within a 12-month and 24-month period. Convictions may be assigned three, four or six demerit points.
items.mnemonic: Points come in 3, 4 or 6. DMV counts 12 and 24 months.

items.title: Under 18: first ticket means clinic
items.simple: If you are under 18 and get a point, seat belt or child seat conviction, you must finish a driver improvement clinic within 90 days. If you do not, your license is suspended until you finish and pay a fee.
items.official: If you are convicted of a demerit point traffic violation (or safety belt/child restraint violation) committed when you were under age 18, DMV will require that you complete a driver improvement clinic. If you do not complete the clinic within 90 days, DMV will suspend your driving privilege until you complete the clinic and pay a reinstatement fee.
items.mnemonic: First ticket under 18: class within 90 days.

items.title: Under 18, second ticket: 90 days
items.simple: If you are under 18 and get a second point or seat belt conviction, DMV suspends your license for 90 days.
items.official: After your second conviction for a demerit point traffic violation (or safety belt/child restraint violation) committed when you were under age 18, DMV will suspend your driving privilege for 90 days.
items.mnemonic: Ticket 1: class. Ticket 2: 90 days. Ticket 3: revoked.

items.title: Under 18, third ticket: revoked
items.simple: If you are under 18 and get a third conviction, your license is revoked for one year or until you turn 18. The revocation lasts for whichever is longer.
items.official: Your third conviction will result in a revocation of your driving privilege for one year or until you reach age 18, whichever is longer.
items.mnemonic: Strike 3: out 1 year or until 18, whichever is longer.

items.title: Age 18 or 19: clinic
items.simple: If you are 18 or 19 and are convicted of a point, seat belt or child seat violation, DMV makes you take a driver improvement clinic.
items.official: DMV will require you to complete a driver improvement clinic if you are convicted of a demerit point or safety belt/child restraint violation committed while you were age 18 or 19.
items.mnemonic: Still a teen? One ticket means a class.

items.title: Adults: clinic at 12 or 18
items.simple: If you are 18 or older, DMV requires a driver improvement clinic when you get 12 points in 12 months or 18 points in 24 months. You must finish it within 90 days, or your license is suspended.
items.official: DMV will require you to complete a driver improvement clinic if you accumulate 12 demerit points within 12 months or 18 points within 24 months. If you do not complete the clinic within 90 days, DMV will suspend your driving privilege.
items.mnemonic: 12 in 12 or 18 in 24: go to class.

items.title: Adults: 18 or 24 points suspended
items.simple: If you get 18 points in 12 months or 24 points in 24 months, DMV suspends your license for 90 days. You must also complete a driver improvement clinic.
items.official: If you receive 18 demerit points within 12 months or 24 points within 24 months, DMV will suspend your driving privilege for 90 days and require that you complete a driver improvement clinic.
items.mnemonic: 18 in 12 or 24 in 24: 90 days parked.

items.title: Medical review program
items.simple: If DMV hears that a health problem may keep you from driving safely, it may do a medical review. The review looks at your alertness, vision, judgment and motor skills. You may need a doctor's report or DMV tests.
items.official: When DMV receives a report that a driver may have a physical or mental condition that affects his ability to drive safely, a medical review of the driver may be conducted. DMV is concerned about any condition that impairs the driver's level of consciousness, perception (vision), judgment, motor skills. DMV may require you to submit a medical or vision report completed by your physician and/or to pass the two-part knowledge exam and/or road skills test.
items.mnemonic: Awake, see, think, move.

items.title: Medical review results
items.simple: After a medical review, DMV may suspend your license or limit it. DMV may ask for doctor reports from time to time. DMV may also end the review with no other requirements.
items.official: Once the medical review is completed, DMV will decide whether to: suspend your driving privilege; restrict your driving privilege; require you to submit periodic medical and/or vision reports; or end the medical review with no other requirements. If DMV suspends your driving privilege as a result of medical review action, you will not be required to present legal presence proof documents to reinstate your driving privilege unless required to do so for another suspension/revocation or your license expires.

items.title: Insurance or the $500 fee
items.simple: To register a car and get plates, you need one of two things. You need liability insurance, or you must pay the $500 uninsured motor vehicle fee. Buy your insurance from a company allowed to do business in Virginia.
items.official: To register a vehicle and obtain license plates, you must have liability insurance or pay the $500 uninsured motor vehicle fee. Insure your vehicle with a company authorized to do business in Virginia. When registering a motor vehicle, you must sign a statement on the registration application that you have liability insurance coverage for your motor vehicle, or pay the $500 uninsured motor vehicle fee.
items.mnemonic: $500 to register without insurance. $600 if caught driving without it.

items.title: The $500 fee is not insurance
items.simple: Paying the $500 uninsured motor vehicle fee does NOT give you insurance. It only lets you register and drive the car in Virginia for one year.
items.official: Paying the uninsured motor vehicle fee does not provide insurance coverage, but it allows you to register and operate the vehicle in Virginia for a one-year period.
items.mnemonic: The fee buys time, not protection.

items.title: Insurance checks and your plates
items.simple: DMV checks that cars are insured. DMV suspends your license if you do not send insurance information when asked. It also suspends your license if your insurance stops and you do not return your plates.
items.official: DMV will suspend your driving privilege if: you do not submit the requested insurance policy information to verify that you have liability insurance coverage; there is a break in your insurance policy coverage and you do not return your license plates to DMV.
items.mnemonic: Insurance stops? Plates go back to DMV.

items.title: Insure the whole registration period
items.simple: Keep a registered car insured for the whole registration period. Do this even if you never drive the car or it does not run. Before you cancel insurance, return the plates to DMV and cancel the registration.
items.official: Insure your Virginia-registered vehicle during the entire registration period even if it is not driven or is inoperable. Before you cancel your insurance, return the license plates to DMV and cancel the registration.
items.mnemonic: Plates on the car? Insurance on the car.

items.title: Caught uninsured: $600 and 3 years
items.simple: If you are caught driving uninsured and did not pay the $500 fee, DMV suspends your license. To get it back, pay a $600 fee or get approved for a payment plan. Your insurer must file proof for 3 years.
items.official: If you are caught driving without insurance and you did not pay the uninsured motor vehicle fee, DMV will suspend your driving privilege until you pay a $600 noncompliance fee or apply and be approved for a payment plan, and have your insurance company file a certificate that you have a policy with the required coverage limits. You will have to file this certificate of insurance for three years from the date you regain your driving privileges.
items.mnemonic: Caught uninsured: $600, then 3 years of proof.

items.title: Minimum liability: 30/60/20
items.simple: For policies starting on or after January 1, 2022, the minimum liability coverage is $30,000 for one person hurt or killed, $60,000 for two or more people hurt or killed, and $20,000 for property damage.
items.official: At a minimum, your insurance policy must provide the following liability insurance coverage. Policies effective on or after Jan. 1, 2022: injury or death of one person $30,000; injury or death of two or more people $60,000; property damage $20,000. (Policies effective before Jan. 1, 2022: $25,000, $50,000, $20,000.) In some cases, liability insurance requirements may be higher.
items.mnemonic: 30 for one, double it (60) for more, 20 for property.

items.title: Child support: 90 days or $5,000
items.simple: If you are 90 days late or $5,000 behind on child support, your license can be suspended. Missing a child support or paternity court date can also lead to suspension. Ignoring court papers about those hearings can do the same.
items.official: The Division of Child Support Enforcement will direct DMV to suspend your driving privilege if you are late making child support payments by 90 days or $5,000, or fail to appear in court or comply with a subpoena, summons or warrant related to paternity or child support hearings.
items.mnemonic: 90 days or 5 thousand: license on hold.

items.title: Household drivers affect insurance cost
items.simple: Insurance companies may look at the driving records of everyone of driving age in your home. A newly licensed driver may change what your policy costs. Ask your insurance agent about it.
items.official: Insurance companies may factor in their policy premium the driving records of any individual of driving age that resides within an insured's household. If you have any questions regarding the potential impact a newly licensed driver may have on your policy, you may wish to contact your insurance agent.
items.mnemonic: Your record rides on the family policy.
